Where do the multi-cycle conditions (`feed_stale` >3 cycles, cap pinned 2 cycles, pace error >15% for 2 cycles) get evaluated?** Since `govern()` is pure and already tracks a feed-stale counter for the 3-cycle fallback (SPEC.md:50-52), extend that same pattern: add cap-pinned and pace-error counters to the persisted controller state, and have `govern()` return an `alerts: [...]` list alongside `cap`/`state`/`guardrail`. That keeps every alert condition deterministic, unit-testable, and replayable by the simulation harness — the same ladder that already covers guardrails covers alerting. The alternative (tracking cycle history in a stateful wrapper around the supervisor) works but duplicates state outside the tested core and can drift from what `govern()` "sees."

**2. Heartbeat-missed is fundamentally different and can't live in this design at all.** If the loop doesn't run, no code inside the loop can notice. That needs an external dead-man's-switch: persist a last-successful-cycle timestamp per tenant, and have something outside the tenant loop (a monitoring check, Healthchecks.io/Cronitor-style ping, or a Prometheus `absent()`-style rule) alert when it goes stale past 5 minutes + margin.

With that split, the supervisor loop becomes a thin dispatcher: call `govern()`, persist state, apply the cap, then fire `alert(...)` for each entry in `result.alerts` (single-cycle guardrails like `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `config_invalid` are just one-element cases of the same list). Left out: the actual alert sink/transport (pager vs. Slack vs. metric) and de-dup/throttling policy so a stuck tenant doesn't page every 5 minutes — that's a level below what SPEC.md specifies.

Grounded in the actual code: every write in this service already funnels through one place, `db.write()` in `db.js:13`, and every request already gets `req.user` resolved by `sessionUser` in `auth.js:5` before any route runs. That's the whole audit trail problem already half-solved by the existing architecture.

**Core design**

Add an `audit_log` table (`table_name`, `row_id`, `action`, `actor_id`, `actor_email`, `occurred_at`, `old_row jsonb`, `new_row jsonb`) and two complementary capture points:

1. **App-level, in `write()`**: change its signature to accept the acting user, e.g. `db.write(sql, params, req.user)`. Inside the existing transaction, run `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = $1` before the write, then `SELECT` the pre-image (for UPDATE/DELETE) and rely on the `RETURNING *` already used everywhere for the post-image. Both go into `audit_log` in the same transaction, so audit and mutation commit or roll back together.
2. **DB-level triggers**: `AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` row triggers on `accounts`, `orders`, etc. that write to `audit_log` themselves, reading the actor off `current_setting('app.actor_id', true)`. This is what actually guarantees "for every write" — it fires even if a future route handler calls `pool.query` directly instead of `db.write()`, or someone runs a migration or a manual `psql` fix.

The two aren't redundant: the trigger is the enforcement mechanism, the app-level `SET LOCAL` is how it learns who did it, since Postgres has no notion of your application's session users.

**The one real fork**: whether you need trigger-level enforcement at all, or whether app-level-only (just instrumenting `write()`) is enough. That depends on whether anything writes to this database outside this service — other services, ops scripts, a console. If this service is the sole writer and the team will hold the line on routing all writes through `db.write()`, app-level capture is simpler and gets you 90% of the value with no DDL/trigger maintenance. If compliance means "no write can happen without a trail, full stop," you need the trigger backstop.

**Left out of this design, worth deciding separately**: making `audit_log` genuinely append-only (revoke UPDATE/DELETE from the app's DB role, since a trail that can be edited isn't a trail), retention/export policy, and whether reads also need to be logged (you asked about writes only, so I didn't design for that).

The CDN is already sitting in front of every request, fully obeys `Cache-Control`, and is at 0% hit rate — not because caching wasn't built, but because `middleware/security.js` slaps `no-store, no-cache, private` on every response app-wide (app.js:9). That blanket rule exists for `/account/orders`, which is genuinely per-user and must never be cached by an intermediary. It got applied to `/p/:slug` too, but that page is anonymous and identical for everyone — `db.js` even notes "Nothing here is per-user."

So the fix isn't a new caching layer, it's un-suppressing the one that's already there: split the header policy per route instead of setting it once for everything. `/account` keeps exactly what it has now. `/p/:slug` gets something like `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=600` — catalog rows only change a few times a day, so that's a comfortable margin, and it collapses the ~890ms of `relatedProducts` + `stockFor` + `productBySlug` to a CDN hit for every repeat request in that window, no app or DB code touched.

One thing I can't resolve without more context: `stockFor` is bundled into the same page render as catalog copy, but stock is more staleness-sensitive than a product description — a 5-minute `s-maxage` risks showing "in stock" briefly after a sellout. Worth deciding whether that's acceptable or whether stock needs its own shorter TTL (or a client-side fetch that bypasses the cached page).

Left out at this level: purge-on-write when the admin tool edits a product (vs. just letting the TTL expire), and app-level caching (Redis, etc.) for whatever still misses the edge — that's only worth adding after headers are fixed and you can see the real miss rate.

**SSE (Server-Sent Events)** over WebSockets: the dashboard only needs server→client pushes, not bidirectional traffic, so SSE gets you auto-reconnect and plain-HTTP simplicity without the extra protocol overhead. Backend emits an event whenever the underlying data changes (or a lightweight poller diffs and emits), and the client patches just the changed rows/cards instead of refetching the whole dashboard. Polling with a short interval is the fallback if the backend can't cheaply detect changes — simpler to build, less real-time.

What's the current stack (backend language/framework)? That decides whether SSE is a few lines or needs a library, and whether "detect changes" means a DB trigger, a queue subscription, or just a cheap periodic diff.

The current flow in `routes/checkout.js` and `payments.js` treats any thrown error — including a timeout — as a hard failure and returns 502. But `PROVIDER.md` is explicit that a timeout is **unknown**, not failed, and that Cardstream supports `Idempotency-Key` for exactly this case. The bug isn't "no retry loop," it's that retrying without an idempotency key on this endpoint is unsafe (could double-charge), and right now no key is ever sent.

**Core design:** generate a stable key per payment attempt — `pay-${order.id}` is enough here, since `status !== 'pending'` already guards against a second checkout call reusing the row — and send it as `Idempotency-Key` on the charge and on every retry of that same charge. On `timeout`/`ECONNRESET` specifically, retry a couple of times with backoff (2-3 attempts is plenty given the 600/min limit); on a real decline (4xx from the provider), don't retry, that's a genuine failure. This turns "retry" from risky into safe, because Cardstream dedupes on the key.

**The one fork worth deciding:** what happens if retries are exhausted and it's still unknown. Two options:
- Keep it synchronous — retry inline within the request, and if still unresolved after retries, return something other than "payment failed" (e.g. "processing", HTTP 202) and reconcile the order status later via a background check against the same idempotency key.
- Go fully async — mark the order `processing` before the first attempt, return immediately, and let a worker own the charge+retry+reconcile loop, with checkout only polling for the outcome.

Given the volume described ("a few times a day"), inline retry with a fallback to a `processing`/`payment_unknown` order status (instead of `paid`/`pending`/failure) is the smaller change and avoids ever showing "failed" for something that might actually have succeeded. The async worker is the more robust version if timeouts get more frequent or retries need to survive a server restart.

Since there's no existing codebase here to anchor on, the answer depends on scale and current stack — what database/backend are you already running?

The core approach either way: index product name + description into a search-friendly structure (not `LIKE '%term%'`, which can't rank or scale), tokenize the query, and rank matches by relevance instead of just filtering.

The one real fork is where that index lives:
- **Same database** (Postgres `tsvector`/GIN index, or trigram via `pg_trgm` for typo tolerance) — no new infra, fine up to roughly hundreds of thousands of products, good enough relevance for a first version.
- **Dedicated search engine** (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, or hosted like Algolia/Typesense/Meilisearch) — needed if you want strong typo-tolerance, synonym handling, or the catalog is large/growing fast. Costs you a second system to keep in sync with product updates.

For a first version of "type a few words, get matches," I'd default to the in-database option unless you already know you need fuzzy/typo-tolerant ranking or the catalog is large.

Depth left out: keeping the index in sync on product create/update (trigger vs. async job), and ranking tuning (boosting name matches over description matches).

Recommended shape: client compresses/resizes each photo before sending (phone shots run 3–12MB and need orientation/HEIC handling anyway), then uploads directly to object storage via a presigned URL rather than through your app server, and the backend registers the photo against the listing and generates thumbnails asynchronously once the object lands (e.g. via a storage-trigger job).

Two decisions that actually fork the design:

- **Where resizing happens.** Client-side (canvas/native resize before upload) cuts upload time and mobile data use, which matters directly for "phone camera size," but adds client complexity — especially HEIC-to-JPEG conversion on iOS. Server-side resizing keeps the client dumb but means uploading full-size originals over mobile networks first.
- **Upload path.** Direct-to-storage via presigned URL scales better and keeps large binaries off your app server. Proxying through the app server is simpler for auth/validation/limits but makes your server a bandwidth/cost bottleneck as sellers upload more photos.

Left out below this level: retry/resume behavior for flaky mobile uploads, EXIF stripping for privacy, and how multi-photo ordering/primary-photo selection is modeled.
